title: Constantinople falls (1453)
hookLine: the last liturgy in Hagia Sophia; the Orthodox world's center shifts north

lines: ONE MORE SERVICE UNDER THE DOME.
cards: Candles, a great dome overhead, and a crowd with every reason to be afraid. The city is under siege. Outside, an army has pounded the walls with cannon, day after day.
On the last evening, the old accounts say, the people of Constantinople crowd into their great church for one more service.
Greek Christians and Latin Christians, who had quarreled bitterly, stand under the same dome and pray together. Some confess their sins. Some ask forgiveness of the person next to them.
Then the soldiers go back to the walls.

teach.b: The church was Hagia Sophia, Holy Wisdom, long the heart of Eastern Christianity: the seat of the patriarch, the place where emperors were crowned. The army outside belonged to the Ottoman sultan, Mehmed.
When the walls broke, the emperor, Constantine, died fighting at them, the accounts say, and the city that called itself the new Rome passed into Ottoman hands.
Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia, and before long it was a mosque, with Muslim prayer under the same dome. People still tell a story about that last liturgy.

teach.h: THE PRIEST WHO WALKED INTO THE WALL.
teach.b: As soldiers burst in, the story goes, a priest at the altar picked up the holy gifts and walked into the wall, and the wall closed behind him. One day, the story says, he will walk out and finish the service.
It's told as legend, not history: the kind of story people tell when something unfinished hurts. A Psalm knows that hurt.
In the King James Bible: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." But the Orthodox world didn't end; its center moved.

teach.h: THE CENTER MOVES NORTH. SOME STAY.
teach.b: In the north, Russian Christians began to see themselves as carriers of what Constantinople had held, and some in Moscow spoke of a third Rome. And in the old city, Christians stayed.
The patriarchate went on, with a new patriarch installed under the new rulers, and the Orthodox lived as a minority, keeping their churches and their liturgy, generation after generation.
The last liturgy in Hagia Sophia was not the last liturgy.

how: Orthodox Christians remember the fall of Constantinople with sorrow, and the Ecumenical Patriarch, honored by Orthodox Christians as first among their patriarchs, still has his seat in the city, now Istanbul.

the Western church breaking away from the East

games.q: you're a Christian in Constantinople on the last evening. the walls won't hold much longer. where do you go?
o: go to Hagia Sophia for one more service, beside people you once quarreled with.
games.why: the old accounts say the people crowded into the great church, Greek and Latin together, and prayed before the soldiers went back to the walls.

practice: Hold in mind Christians who live as a small community, among neighbors who mostly follow another faith or none: a small church on an ordinary street, a few families keeping it going year after year.
If you know one by name, bring it to mind. If you pray, pray for them; if you don't, simply wish them well, and their neighbors too.

wordCard.voice: Constantinople falls. The great Christian city of the East passes to the Ottomans, Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque, and Orthodox Christians carry on, in the old city and in the north.

orig.note: Greek: holy wisdom, the name of the great church of Constantinople.

carryVoice: Your line: the last liturgy. The city fell, and the people who prayed there kept going. Day eight hundred thirty-seven, done.
